catalog_quote: Yaur has both contrastive tone and vowel length.[fn. 21: Yaur was not known to be tonal prior to my fieldwork.] There is rarely more than one long vowel in a word. The tone-bearing unit is the mora, with short vowels counted as a single mora, and long vowels and diphthongs counted as two moras. Two underlying tones are associated with moras: high (H) and low (L). It follows that contour tones can be realized only as the sequences HL and LH on long vowels and diphthongs. Most of my Yaur lexicon of 1342 words consists of disyllables and trisyllables. Although various tone patterns are attested, there are only four common patterns on disyllables and six on trisyllables. ... An example of a near-minimal disyllabic quadruplet is hníoojè ‘body hair’, òojé ‘sugarcane’, óòjé ‘head louse’, and ’òórè ‘bone’. To this set may be added òjé ‘bamboo’, illustrating the vowel length contrast. [p. 9 fn. 3] Whether what I analyze as length or tone could be reanalyzed as stress (more plausible in some cases than others) has little impact on the complexity of the system and the care with which it must be examined. [p. 8] At least six SHWNG languages are known to be tonal: the Raja Ampat languages Ma'ya, Matbat, and Ambel (Remijsen 2001; Arnold forthcoming) and the southern Cenderawasih Bay languages Moor, Yerisiam, and Yaur (own fieldwork). [Table 17, p. 28] Yaur • No robust generalizations.

Two underlying tones are associated with moras: high (H) and low (L). It follows that contour tones can be realized only as the sequences HL and LH on long vowels and diphthongs.' with fn. 21 'Yaur was not known to be tonal prior to my fieldwork.' p. 3 (= p. 9) fn. 3 reads exactly 'Whether what I analyze as length or…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Yaur is described as a lexical tone language (H vs L per mora) with contrastive vowel length; the only modern description gives no word-stress rule and does not posit stress, noting only that some length/tone facts might alternatively be analysed as stress. Unlike its sister Yerisiam and neighbour Moor, no reflex of Proto-SHWNG penultimate stress is identified for Yaur ('no robust generalizations', Table 17 p. 28; diss. p. 117).
new_statements.exceptions: Author flags the analysis as 'a work in progress' (p. 10): in Yaur suprasegmental contrasts are neutralised in many phonological contexts, production is variable, and speakers treat the contrasts as optional (p. 9). Common tone patterns: disyllables H-L 202, L-H 176, HL-H 42, LH-L 36; trisyllables H-H-L 167, L-L-H 119, etc. (Table 13 p. 26).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical (word-level) tone on citation forms from a 1342-word lexicon; no phrase-level prosody described.
new_statements.identity_note: Kamholz's Yaur data are from his own 2010-2013 fieldwork (speakers from the Sima/Yaur coast, Nabire regency); the language-level glottocode yaur1239 applies directly, no dialect split is described. Yaur forms the Yaur-Yerisiam subgroup (yaur1240) with Yerisiam (ires1239), whose Kamholz files are the same PDFs held under (hard-linked here).

tone_statements.citation: Kaufman, Daniel & Nikolaus P. Himmelmann. 2024. Suprasegmental phonology. In Alexander Adelaar & Antoinette Schapper (eds.), The Oxford Guide to the Malayo-Polynesian Languages of Southeast Asia, 703-718. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
tone_statements.quote: This contrasts with Moor, which is analysed by Kamholz (2014:101–106) as having four tonal patterns, largely confined to the final two syllables. More importantly, and rather unusually for a tone language, “tones are realized only on phrase-final words” (Kamholz 2014:102). Kamholz (2014:116 passim) also briefly mentions Yerisiam and Yaur as languages with a complex word tone system plus contrastive vowel length. A particularly complex – and cross-linguistically unusual – word-prosodic system is found in Ma'ya, spoken on the Raja Ampat Islands.

sources.note: Yaur analysed as a tone language with contrastive vowel length (TBU = mora, underlying H and L); no synchronic word-stress statement. p. 117 lists SHWNG languages with penultimate stress or traces of it (Ma'ya, Moor, Yerisiam, Buli, Sawai, Taba, Ambai, Wandamen, Waropen, Warembori) -- Yaur is not among them.
